title: Type-A Hecke Specht Modules and Cellular Bases

items.title: Cellular bases and cell modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.
items.strategy: A definition item recording the Graham-Lehrer axioms exactly as used later. The only point needing care is that the displayed formula really defines a module action: this is Corollary 2.3(i) of the source, obtained by applying the anti-automorphism (i) to the triangular relation; the ideal identification is the display after (2.5). In every application on this page $A=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ is a free $R$-module of finite rank. No choice is used.

items.title: e-regular and e-restricted partitions
items.statement:
Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For prime $e=p$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]; the same inequalities define the
extension to composite finite $e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).
items.strategy: A definition item specialising the published $p$-regular/$p$-restricted definitions along the prime $p=e$; the conjugate equivalence is the finite-$e$ case of the corresponding statement for partitions ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]). No choice is used.

items.title: The quantum characteristic of an invertible Hecke parameter
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{	imes}$ an invertible element. The **quantum characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that $1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]], [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1
e0$, the least positive integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so the two formulations coincide. Concretely: (i) if $q
e1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$, so a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{	imes}$; (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ and $e=\infty$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]). If $e<\infty$ then $q
e1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every integer $m$; in particular the quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition item; the identities $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for $q\ne1$ and $[m]_1=m$ are the definition of the quantum integers, and the displayed equivalences are immediate case checks. The last sentence records the reduction $[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q$ that every later residue computation uses. No choice is used.

items.title: Decompositions of the identity into primitive central idempotents are unique
items.statement: Let $A$ be a unital ring, with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$ where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$; in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.
items.strategy: For each pair, $e_if_j$ is an idempotent (all factors commute) and $\sum_j e_if_j=e_i$ with pairwise orthogonal terms; primitivity of $e_i$ forces all but one term to vanish, say $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}$. Symmetrically each $f_j$ admits exactly one $i$ with $f_j=f_je_i$. The map $i\mapsto j(i)$ is injective (otherwise some $f_j$ would split as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents), and counting the two decompositions of $1$ shows that it is a bijection; then $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}=f_{j(i)}e_i=f_{j(i)}$ because all idempotents involved are central, so the families coincide. No choice is used.

items.title: The identity of a finite-dimensional algebra decomposes into primitive central idempotents
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional
commutative $F$-algebra, and the identity $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents of $A$: each $e_i$ is a
nonzero idempotent of $Z(A)$ that is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal
idempotents of $Z(A)$. No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed and no choice
principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra $A$, and the centre $C:=Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$.

[F1] $F$-algebra conventions: a unital $F$-algebra $A$ is a unital ring together with a unital ring homomorphism $\eta:F\to A$ whose image is central, and the induced scalar action $ra:=\eta(r)a$ makes $A$ an $F$-module with multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[F2] Subspace dimension: if $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ with $\dim_FV=n$ and $U$ a linear subspace of $V$, then $U$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim_FU\le n$, and $\dim_FU=n$ if and only if $U=V$ ([[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]).

[F3] Well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $A=0$, then $C=Z(A)=\{0\}$ and the empty family ($k=0$) satisfies $1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$ with the stated conditions vacuously, so assume $A\ne0$; then in $A$ one has $1\ne0$ and hence $1\ne0$ in $C$. [given, F1]

1.2 The centre $C$ is a commutative unital $F$-subalgebra of $A$ and, in particular, a linear subspace of the $F$-vector space $A$: $1\in C$; if $x,y\in C$, $\alpha\in F$ and $a\in A$, then $(x+y)a=xa+ya=ax+ay=a(x+y)$, $(\alpha x)a=\alpha(xa)=\alpha(ax)=a(\alpha x)$ and $(xy)a=x(ya)=x(ay)=(xa)y=(ax)y=a(xy)$, while $0\in C$; and distinct elements of $C$ commute with each other because each commutes with all of $A$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 Suppose, for contradiction, that the following general claim fails: every finite-dimensional commutative unital $F$-algebra $D$ with $1_D\ne0$ and $\dim_FD\ge1$ admits a decomposition of $1_D$ into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of $D$ that are primitive in $D$. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb N$ be the nonempty set of $F$-dimensions of such counterexamples; by [F3] let $d\in S$ be least and fix a counterexample $D$ with $\dim_FD=d$. [given, F3]

2.1 The centre $C$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_FC\le\dim_FA$, by [F2] applied to the linear subspace $C$ of the finite-dimensional space $A$. [step 1.2, F2]

2.2 Since $D$ is a counterexample, $1_D$ is not primitive in $D$: otherwise $k=1$, $e_1=1_D$ would be the required decomposition. Hence there are nonzero orthogonal idempotents $u,v\in D$ with $1_D=u+v$. [step 1.3, given]

3.1 The set $D_u:=uD=\{ux:x\in D\}$ is a linear subspace of $D$ and, with the inherited operations, a commutative unital $F$-algebra with identity $u$: it is closed since $ux+uy=u(x+y)$, $\alpha(ux)=u(\alpha x)$ and $(ux)(uy)=u^2xy=u(xy)$ for $x,y\in D$, $\alpha\in F$, while $u\cdot ux=ux$; and $u\ne0$. The same holds for $D_v:=vD$ with identity $v$. [step 2.2, F1, algebra]

4.1 One has $D_u\ne D$ because $v\notin D_u$: if $v=ux$ then $0=uv=u^2x=ux=v\ne0$, a contradiction using $uv=0$ and $u^2=u$. Hence by [F2], applied to the subspace $D_u$ of $D$ with $\dim_FD=d$, one has $\dim_FD_u<d$; the same argument gives $\dim_FD_v<d$. [step 3.1, step 1.3, F2, algebra]

5.1 By the minimality of $d$ in $S$, no counterexample has dimension $<d$, and since $\dim_FD_u<d$ and $\dim_FD_v<d$ with $1_{D_u}=u\ne0$, $1_{D_v}=v\ne0$, the general claim holds for $D_u$ and for $D_v$: there are pairwise orthogonal idempotents $f_1,\dots,f_a$ of $D_u$ primitive in $D_u$ with $u=f_1+\cdots+f_a$, and pairwise orthogonal idempotents $g_1,\dots,g_b$ of $D_v$ primitive in $D_v$ with $v=g_1+\cdots+g_b$. [step 4.1, step 1.3, given]

6.1 The combined family $f_1,\dots,f_a,g_1,\dots,g_b$ is a decomposition of $1_D$ into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of $D$ that are primitive in $D$: the elements lie in $D_u\cup D_v\subseteq D$; distinct $f$'s are orthogonal and distinct $g$'s are orthogonal by step 5.1; $f_ig_j=(uf_i)(vg_j)=uvf_ig_j=0$; and if $f_i=p+q$ with $p,q$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $D$, then $p=f_ip=uf_ip=up\in D_u$ and likewise $q=uq\in D_u$, contradicting primitivity of $f_i$ in $D_u$ (and symmetrically for $g_j$ in $D_v$). [step 5.1, step 3.1, algebra]

7.1 Step 6.1 contradicts the choice of $D$ as a counterexample, so no counterexample exists and the general claim of step 1.3 holds: every finite-dimensional commutative unital $F$-algebra $D$ with $1_D\ne0$ and $\dim_FD\ge1$ decomposes its identity into pairwise orthogonal primitive idempotents. [step 6.1, step 1.3]

8.1 Apply step 7.1 to $D=C=Z(A)$: by steps 1.1 and 1.2, $C$ is a commutative unital $F$-algebra with $1\ne0$ and $\dim_FC\ge1$; by step 2.1 it is finite-dimensional. This produces $1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$ with the $e_i$ pairwise orthogonal idempotents of $C=Z(A)$ primitive in $C$; idempotents of $Z(A)$ are exactly the central idempotents of $A$, and primitive in $C$ says precisely that $e_i$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $Z(A)$. Since no semisimplicity was used and the only invoked principles are the choice-free subspace theorem [F2], the choice-free well-ordering principle [F3] and finite selections, the proof is complete. [step 7.1, step 2.1, step 1.1] ∎

items.title: The star anti-automorphism of the type-A Hecke algebra
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the specialized type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and relations $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, the braid relations and the distant commutations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Then the assignment $T_i\mapsto T_i$ ($1\le i<n$) extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra anti-automorphism $*:H\to H$, i.e. an $R$-linear map with $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$ and $1^*=1$; it is an involution, $**=\mathrm{id}_H$, and on the standard basis $$T_w^{*}=T_{w^{-1}}\qquad(w\in S_n).$$ In particular $(T_wT_{w^{-1}})^*=T_wT_{w^{-1}}$ and, for the symmetrizers $m_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, one has $m_\lambda^*=m_\lambda$.
items.strategy: The presentation ideal of $H$ is stable under reversal of products: the quadratic, braid and distant-commutation relators are palindromic, so the universal property of the presented algebra applied to $H^{\mathrm{op}}$ yields a unique algebra homomorphism $H\to H^{\mathrm{op}}$ sending each $T_i$ to $T_i$, i.e. an anti-automorphism $*$ of $H$. Since $*$ fixes a generating set, $**$ fixes a generating set and hence is the identity. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one has $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}$ by definition, so $T_w^*=T_{i_\ell}\cdots T_{i_1}=T_{w^{-1}}$, the reversed word being reduced for $w^{-1}$. This is Mathas, Chapter 3 section 2, where $*$ is the $R$-linear antiautomorphism determined by $T_i^*=T_i$ and $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$; no choice is used.

items.title: Blocks of a finite-dimensional algebra via primitive central idempotents
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.
items.strategy: A definition item whose consistency is supplied by its dependencies: the preceding primitive-idempotent decomposition lemma applied to the commutative finite-dimensional $F$-algebra $Z(A)$ produces the primitive central idempotents (its primitive idempotents are exactly the primitive central idempotents of $A$), and the uniqueness lemma makes the block partition canonical. The module decomposition is idempotent calculus: $\sum_ie_i=1$ gives $M=\sum_ie_iM$, orthogonality gives directness, and a nonzero simple $S$ has $e_iS=S$ whenever $e_iS\ne0$. This avoids the Artinian structure theorem and hence uses no choice principle. The conventions follow Mathas, Chapter 5 section 3 (printed pp. 53-54).

items.title: Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$(q-1)[m]_q=q^m-1$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. When $q-1$ is a unit this
may be written $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$; the polynomial definition requires no
such division. Also $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
isomorphism given by the Coxeter presentation and the standard bases
([[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) — sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

items.title: Murphy elements and Murphy tableau elements
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

No choice is used.

items.title: The cell form is associative and its radical is a submodule
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, a cellular $R$-algebra $A$ with cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$, a label $\lambda\in\Lambda$, and the cell module $C^\lambda$ with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:t\in T(\lambda)\}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]).

[F1] The cellular axioms and cell-module structure ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]): $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}\}$ is an $R$-basis of $A$; $A^{\rhd\lambda}=\langle c^{\mu}_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\rangle_R$; the $R$-linear map $i$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$ is an algebra anti-automorphism with $i^2=\mathrm{id}$; for all $\lambda$, $t\in T(\lambda)$, $a\in A$ there are $r_v\in R$ with $c^{\lambda}_{st}a\equiv\sum_{v}r_vc^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ for all $s$; $C^{\lambda}$ is a right $A$-module by $c^{\lambda}_ta:=\sum_vr_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when $c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_vr_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and a left $A$-module via $i$ with $a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_ti(a)$; and $A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_RC^{\lambda}$ via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$, where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}=\langle c^{\mu}_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\rangle_R$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The submodules $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ and $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ are two-sided ideals of $A$, and the following two congruence rules hold modulo $A^{\rhd\lambda}$: for all $a\in A$ and $u,v\in T(\lambda)$, $$c^{\lambda}_{us}a\equiv\sum_{w\in T(\lambda)}r_w\,c^{\lambda}_{uw},\qquad a\,c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\sum_{w\in T(\lambda)}s_w\,c^{\lambda}_{wv},$$ where the $r_w$ do not depend on $u$ and the $s_w$ do not depend on $v$. Indeed, the first is the cellular rule [F1] applied to the fixed label $\lambda$, the second-slot index $s$ and the element $a$, which gives coefficients independent of the free first index $u$; right multiplication by $a$ therefore preserves each $A^{\unrhd\mu}$ and $A^{\rhd\mu}$, so $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ and (as its span over all $\mu\rhd\lambda$) $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ are right ideals, while applying the anti-automorphism $i$ to the first rule — it swaps the two indices, fixes $R$ and preserves both spans — gives the second rule and shows that they are also left ideals. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Existence and uniqueness of the form: for all $s,t\in T(\lambda)$ there is a unique $r=r(s,t)\in R$ with $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv r\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ for all $u,v$, and $r$ depends only on $s,t$. Since $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ is a two-sided ideal by step 1.1, the quotient ring $A/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ contains $Q:=A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ with $R$-basis the classes $\bar c_{uv}:=c^{\lambda}_{uv}+A^{\rhd\lambda}$. Applying the two rules of step 1.1 to the product $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}$ — first with $a:=c^{\lambda}_{tv}$, then with $a:=c^{\lambda}_{us}$ — gives $$\bar c_{us}\bar c_{tv}=\sum_w\rho_w\bar c_{uw}=\sum_x\sigma_x\bar c_{xv},$$ where $\rho_w$ does not depend on $u$ and $\sigma_x$ does not depend on $v$. Comparing the coefficients of $\bar c_{ab}$ in the two bases: the left expansion contributes $\rho_b$ when $a=u$ and $0$ otherwise, the right expansion $\sigma_a$ when $b=v$ and $0$ otherwise; hence $\sigma_a=0$ for $a\ne u$ and $\rho_b=0$ for $b\ne v$, leaving $\bar c_{us}\bar c_{tv}=\sigma_u\bar c_{uv}=\rho_v\bar c_{uv}$. The common value $\sigma_u=\rho_v$ is independent of $v$ (being $\sigma_u$) and independent of $u$ (being $\rho_v$), so it depends only on $s,t$; call it $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$. It is determined by the displayed congruence, because the coefficient of $\bar c_{uv}$ in the indicated free basis is unique, including over the zero ring. Bilinear extension gives the unique $R$-bilinear form with the stated property. [given, step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Symmetry: for all $s,t,u,v$, using that $i$ is an anti-automorphism with $i(c^{\lambda}_{ab})=c^{\lambda}_{ba}$, fixes $R$ and preserves $A^{\rhd\lambda}$, one has $$\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}\equiv c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}=(c^{\lambda}_{vt}c^{\lambda}_{su})^{i}\equiv\bigl(\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_{vu}\bigr)^{i}=\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv},$$ so $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle c^{\lambda}_t,c^{\lambda}_s\rangle_\lambda$, and by bilinearity $\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$ for all $x,y\in C^{\lambda}$. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

3.2 Associativity: fix $s,t\in T(\lambda)$ and $a\in A$, and write $c^{\lambda}_s a=\sum_wr_wc^{\lambda}_w$ in $C^{\lambda}$ — the coefficients $r_w$ are those of step 1.1. Then, by step 2.1 applied first to $c^{\lambda}_sa$ and bilinearity of the form, $$\langle c^{\lambda}_sa,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\sum_wr_w\bar c_{uw}\bar c_{tv}=(\bar c_{us}\bar a)\cdot\bar c_{tv}=\bar c_{us}\cdot\bigl(\bar a\bar c_{tv}\bigr).$$ The second rule of step 1.1 writes $ac^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\sum_xs_xc^{\lambda}_{xv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ with coefficients $s_x$ characterised by $c^{\lambda}_ti(a)=\sum_xs_xc^{\lambda}_x$ in $C^{\lambda}$; hence $$\bar c_{us}\cdot\bigl(\bar a\bar c_{tv}\bigr)=\sum_xs_x\bar c_{us}\bar c_{xv}=\sum_xs_x\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_x\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_ti(a)\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\bar c_{uv}.$$ Cancelling the basis element $\bar c_{uv}$ gives $\langle c^{\lambda}_sa,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,i(a)c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$; by bilinearity this is $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $x,y\in C^{\lambda}$. Replacing $a$ by $i(a)$ and using $i^2=\mathrm{id}$ gives the equivalent left-action form $\langle x\,i(a),y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)\cdot y\rangle_\lambda$, where $i(a)\cdot y=y\,i(i(a))=y\,a$ is the left action of $i(a)$: this is the dual statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, algebra]

3.3 The adjointness identity $x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$ holds for all $x\in C^{\lambda}$ and $u,v\in T(\lambda)$: it suffices to treat $x=c^{\lambda}_s$, and there step 2.1 with $(u,s,t,v):=(s,s,u,v)$ gives $c^{\lambda}_{ss}c^{\lambda}_{uv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$; by the definition of the right action in [F1], the coefficients of $c^{\lambda}_{sv}$ on the right are exactly the coefficients of $c^{\lambda}_v$ in $c^{\lambda}_s\cdot c^{\lambda}_{uv}$, so $c^{\lambda}_s\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$; bilinearity in $x$ extends this to all $x$. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 The radical is a submodule and a kernel: for fixed $y\in C^{\lambda}$ the assignment $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda$ is an $R$-linear map with kernel $\{x:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\}$, so $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}=\bigcap_y\ker(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda)$ is an $R$-submodule; and if $x\in\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ then for every $a\in A$ and $y\in C^{\lambda}$ step 3.2 gives $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda=0$, so $xa\in\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$: the radical is an $A$-submodule, namely the kernel of the $A$-module map $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$. This completes the proof of (i)-(iv). [step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra] ∎

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

items.title: Nonzero cell heads classify the simple modules of a cellular algebra
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

items.title: Cellular decomposition matrices are unitriangular for the cell order
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $A$ a finite-dimensional cellular $F$-algebra with cellular
basis $(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$,
$D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]],
[[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).
For $\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda$ with $D^{\mu}\ne0$ let
$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[C^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]$ be the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ as a
composition factor of $C^{\lambda}$ (well defined by
[[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] and
[[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\unrhd\mu,$$
i.e. a nonzero off-diagonal entry can occur only in the allowed direction of the
cell order $\unrhd$ (larger cell first). Order the labels by a linear extension from smaller to larger. The square
submatrix whose rows and columns both have nonzero $D$ is lower
unitriangular; the full rectangular matrix has the same labelled diagonal
and the stated vanishing region. This
determines only the diagonal and the vanishing region: no off-diagonal entry is
computed by cellularity.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra $A$ with cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$, cell modules $C^{\lambda}$ and cell forms $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]).

[F1] Classification ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]): $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$ if and only if $\langle-,-\rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero; in that case $D^{\lambda}$ is simple and $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is its unique maximal submodule, and $\{D^{\lambda}:D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules.

[F2] Cell-form calculus ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]): $c^{\kappa}_{us}c^{\kappa}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\kappa}_s,c^{\kappa}_t\rangle_\kappa c^{\kappa}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\kappa}}$ for a fixed label $\kappa$; $x\,c^{\kappa}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\kappa}_u\rangle_\kappa c^{\kappa}_v$ for $x\in C^{\kappa}$; and $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\kappa}=\{x:\langle x,-\rangle_\kappa=0\}$ is the kernel of $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\kappa$.

[F3] Cellular axioms ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]): $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ is the span of the $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$, $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is the span with $\mu\unrhd\lambda$; condition (ii) reads $c^{\lambda}_{st}a\equiv\sum_vr_vc^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ and its $i$-image reads $ac^{\lambda}_{st}\equiv\sum_ur'_uc^{\lambda}_{ut}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$.

[F4] Composition multiplicities are additive in short exact sequences and well defined by Jordan-Hölder ([[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]], [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Annihilation: if $\lambda,\nu\in\Lambda$ with $\lambda\not\unrhd\nu$, then $A^{\unrhd\nu}\cdot C^{\lambda}=0$. Indeed $A^{\unrhd\nu}$ and $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ are two-sided ideals by [F3], and their intersection is spanned by the $c^{\gamma}$ with $\gamma\unrhd\nu$ and $\gamma\unrhd\lambda$; no such $\gamma$ equals $\lambda$, since $\gamma=\lambda$ would give $\lambda\unrhd\nu$, so the intersection lies in $A^{\rhd\lambda}$. Hence $A^{\unrhd\nu}A^{\unrhd\lambda}\subseteq A^{\unrhd\nu}\cap A^{\unrhd\lambda}\subseteq A^{\rhd\lambda}$ and, since $c^{\lambda}_{tt}\in A^{\unrhd\lambda}$, every product $c^{\lambda}_{tt}b$ with $b\in A^{\unrhd\nu}$ lies in $A^{\rhd\lambda}$; the right action of $b$ on $C^{\lambda}$ is read off from $c^{\lambda}_{tt}b\equiv\sum_vr_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$ with unique coefficients, so $b$ acts as the zero operator on $C^{\lambda}$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Nontrivial action: if $D^{\mu}\ne0$ then some element of $A^{\unrhd\mu}$ acts nontrivially on $D^{\mu}$. Since $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}\ne C^{\mu}$ by [F1], there is $t\in T(\mu)$ with $c^{\mu}_t\notin\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$, and by [F2] there is $u\in T(\mu)$ with $\langle c^{\mu}_t,c^{\mu}_u\rangle_\mu\ne0$; then the element $c^{\mu}_{ut}\in A^{\unrhd\mu}$ satisfies $c^{\mu}_t\cdot c^{\mu}_{ut}=\langle c^{\mu}_t,c^{\mu}_u\rangle_\mu c^{\mu}_t$ by [F2], so on $D^{\mu}$ it sends the nonzero class of $c^{\mu}_t$ to its nonzero multiple $\langle c^{\mu}_t,c^{\mu}_u\rangle_\mu[c^{\mu}_t]\ne0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Off-diagonal vanishing: suppose $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$ with $D^{\mu}\ne0$. If $\lambda\not\unrhd\mu$, then step 1.1 gives $A^{\unrhd\mu}\cdot C^{\lambda}=0$; an element of $A$ acting as zero on a module acts as zero on each of its submodules and quotients, hence on every subquotient of $C^{\lambda}$, so $A^{\unrhd\mu}$ annihilates the composition factor $D^{\mu}$ of $C^{\lambda}$. This contradicts step 1.2. Hence $\lambda\unrhd\mu$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4]

2.2 Diagonal: $d_{\mu\mu}=1$ for every $\mu$ with $D^{\mu}\ne0$. The form radical gives the subquotient $D^{\mu}=C^{\mu}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$, and additivity of composition multiplicities [F4] gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[C^{\mu}:D^{\mu}]=[C^{\mu}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}:D^{\mu}]+[\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}:D^{\mu}]=1+[\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}:D^{\mu}]$, because $C^{\mu}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}=D^{\mu}$ is simple by [F1]. The span of the $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ annihilates $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$: for $x\in\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$ and all $u,v$ one has $x\,c^{\mu}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\mu}_u\rangle_\mu c^{\mu}_v=0$ by [F2]. Hence every element of this span acts as zero on $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$ and on all its subquotients, so $D^{\mu}$ is not a composition factor of $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}$; otherwise step 1.2 would produce an element of $\mathrm{span}\{c^{\mu}_{uv}\}\subseteq A^{\unrhd\mu}$ acting nontrivially on it. Therefore $[\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\mu}:D^{\mu}]=0$ and $d_{\mu\mu}=1$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F4]

3.1 Assembly: order the labels by a linear extension from smaller to larger, and restrict both rows and columns to labels with nonzero form quotient. Step 2.1 puts every nonzero entry on or below the diagonal of this square submatrix, and step 2.2 gives diagonal entries $1$. For the full rectangular matrix retain the label comparison $\lambda\unrhd\mu$; deleting zero-quotient columns need not leave the labelled diagonal on the numerical matrix diagonal. These statements determine only the diagonal and the vanishing region. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

items.title: The type-A Hecke Specht module and its cell form
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.
items.strategy: Keep the fixed-first-index Murphy-cell construction and its local product-defined form above. To check the signed normalization locally, the quadratic relation gives $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$. Therefore $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$ exchanges the two roots $q$ and $-1$ of the quadratic relation. The inverses satisfy the commuting and braid relations, so the scalar multiples $-qT_i^{-1}$ do too; thus $\theta$ is an algebra homomorphism. Applying it twice fixes every generator and proves it is an involutive automorphism. Since $*$ fixes each $T_i$, $\theta$ commutes with the cellular anti-involution. Pullback along this automorphism preserves every submodule, quotient, exact sequence, simplicity and composition multiplicity, and twisting twice is identity. On $M^\theta$ the original form satisfies $\langle x\theta(h),y\rangle=\langle x,y\theta(h)^*\rangle=\langle x,y\theta(h^*)\rangle$, so its radical is unchanged as a subspace. Hence the stated $S$ and $D$ identities are literal consequences of the signed-cell definition, not of an unsupported assertion that taking duals conjugates a label. At $q=1$ all simple transpositions act after pullback with a minus sign, which proves the sign-twist interpretation. For $\lambda=(3)$ at $q=1$ in characteristic zero, $S_{\mathrm M}^{(1^3)}$ has $T_i=-1$; after twisting it has $T_i=1$ as ordinary $S^{(3)}$ must. The printedp25 untwisted conjugate-dual warning is not used as a proof: printedp34 Note3 includes the omitted # twist, while Kleshchev Remark5.5 distinguishes same-shape contragredient duality from sign-twisted conjugation. Identifying this signed-cell construction with every historical Dipper-James polytabloid presentation over arbitrary coefficient rings is a separate proof prerequisite, not silently certified by these source statements.

Fix a beta length $L\ge1$. For a partition $
u$ with at most $L$ columns (that is, $
u_1\le L$), put $$ eta_i(
u)=
u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. items.title: The Jantzen filtration of a lifted cell module
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain ([[def-principal-ideal-domain]]) with a
chosen prime element $\pi$, let $F:=R/\pi R$ be the residue field, and let $M$
be a free $R$-module of finite rank
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]) equipped with a symmetric
$R$-bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:M\times M\to R$ whose extension to the
fraction field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate (equivalently
$\det G\ne0$ for a Gram matrix $G$ of the form). For $i\ge1$ put
$$M(i):=\{x\in M:\langle x,y\rangle\in\pi^iR\ \text{for all }y\in M\},\qquad M_F(i):=(M(i)+\pi M)/\pi M\subseteq M_F:=M\otimes_RF.$$
Then $M(0)=M$, the $M(i)$ are $R$-submodules with $M(i+1)\subseteq M(i)$, the
descending chain
$$M_F=M_F(0)\supseteq M_F(1)\supseteq M_F(2)\supseteq\cdots$$
stabilises at $0$ (that is, $M_F(z)=0$ for all sufficiently large $z$, because
$\det G\ne0$), and $M_F(1)=\mathrm{rad}\,M_F$, the radical of the reduced
form. This finite descending filtration is the **Jantzen filtration** of $M$
with respect to $(R,\pi,\langle\ ,\ \rangle)$. The hypotheses are exactly: $R$
a PID, $\pi$ a prime element, the form non-degenerate over
$\operatorname{Frac}(R)$; no valuation-ring or DVR hypothesis is substituted,
and the prime element $\pi$, its ideal $\pi R$ and the fraction field $K$ are
kept distinct. Each $M(i)$ is a submodule: for the cell forms on this page the
associativity identity $\langle xa,y\rangle=\langle x,ya^*\rangle$ shows
closedness under the action. For $0\ne r\in R$, define $\nu_\pi(r)=\max\{k\ge0:\pi^k\mid r\}$. This maximum is finite: otherwise the uniquely determined elements $r/\pi^k$ give an ascending chain of ideals whose union is principal, say generated by an element in its $N$-th ideal. The chain then stabilizes at $N$, whereas $(r/\pi^N)=(r/\pi^{N+1})$ and cancellation would make $\pi$ a unit. For termination, put $a=\nu_\pi(\det G)$. If $x\in M(i)$, its coordinate column $v$ satisfies $Gv\in\pi^iR^d$, so the adjugate identity gives $(\det G)v\in\pi^iR^d$. For $i>a$, primality of $\pi$ forces every coordinate of $v$ into $\pi R$. Thus $M(i)\subseteq\pi M$ and $M_F(i)=0$. In rank zero the filtration is already zero. Finally a reduced vector belongs to the reduced form radical exactly when any lift pairs with every vector of $M$ into $\pi R$, which is exactly membership in $M(1)$. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The Hecke Jucys-Murphy action is dominance triangular
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its additive Jucys-Murphy elements $L_k$ and its Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with basis $(m_t)$.

[F1] The standard basis multiplication, the quadratic and braid relations, and the integral row action are those of [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. In particular $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, and $x_\rho T_i=q x_\rho$ if $i,i+1$ lie in one row of $t^\rho$.

[F2] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, cell multiplication and finite Garnir straightening are proved in [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. We write $I^{\rhd\lambda}=H^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $x_\lambda=m_\lambda$. The proof there supplies the dominance support rule: if $s'=ss_i$ is standard with $s\rhd s'$ and $\ell(d(s'))=\ell(d(s))+1$, multiplying any same-shape term strictly above $s$ by $T_i$ and then straightening produces only standard terms strictly above $s'$. [F3] A finite-dimensional algebra has nilpotent Jacobson radical and semisimple quotient ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]). A semisimple algebra is a finite product of matrix algebras over division rings ([[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]]); its two-sided ideals and their quotients consequently have no nonzero nilpotent two-sided ideals.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Braid identities.** Put $T_i=T_{(i,i+1)}$. The reduced word for $(j,k+1)$ gives $L_{k+1}=q^{-1}(T_kL_kT_k+T_k)$. We prove $T_iL_k=L_kT_i$ whenever $i\ne k-1,k$. The braid and quadratic relations give $[a,bab]=-q[a,b]$ and $a(baCab)=(baCab)a$ (replace $aba$ by $bab$ and move $C$ past $b$), so its commutator with $a$ vanishes. Thus $L_k$ centralizes $H(S_{k-1})$; since $L_j\in H(S_{k-1})$ for $j<k$, all $L_j$ commute. Multiplying the recurrence by $T_i$ and using $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$ gives $T_iL_{i+1}=L_iT_i+1+(q-1)L_{i+1}$; starring gives $T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-1-(q-1)L_{i+1}$. Hence $T_i$ commutes with $L_i+L_{i+1}$ and $L_iL_{i+1}$: for the product substitute the first identity into $(L_{i+1}T_i-1-(q-1)L_{i+1})L_{i+1}$. items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its Murphy cells $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and form quotients $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, and the ordinary signed-conjugate normalization in the Statement.

[F1] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely simple modules and exhaust the simples. A quotient is nonzero precisely when its form is not identically zero; a zero form quotient makes no assertion about the actual module head ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The actual ordinary module/form bridge gives $S^\lambda=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ and $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$, with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$ an involution commuting with star. Pullback is exact and preserves nonzero modules and simplicity ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Conjugation exchanges regular and restricted partitions ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F3] The locally proved Jucys–Murphy elements commute and preserve a common tableau flag of each Murphy cell, with diagonal word $([c_t(1)]_q,\ldots,[c_t(n)]_q)$, where $c_t(a)$ is the integer node content. The row-filled maximal tableau has an exact eigenrelation ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

[F4] Cellular support gives $[C_{\mathrm M}(\eta):D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)]=0$ unless $\eta\unrhd\rho$, and gives diagonal multiplicity one when that quotient is nonzero ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]).

[F5] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, row action and finite Garnir straightening are valid over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$ and commute with every base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). For a row group $S_\alpha$, $x_\alpha^2=[\alpha]!_Qx_\alpha$ by length-additive parabolic cosets; $[\alpha]!_Q=\prod_j[\alpha_j]!_Q$ ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]).

[F6] At $q=1$, the quantum characteristic is the field characteristic when positive, and is infinity in characteristic zero ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); the ordinary group labels are the regular Specht-head labels ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is the intersection of the annihilators of its simple modules ([[def-jacobson-radical-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed. [F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise. [given, construct, algebra]

1.4 Prove the converse on actual Gram entries. Work in the universal Laurent domain $A$ and write $x_\eta=x_{B_1}\cdots x_{B_k}$ for the symmetrizers of the consecutive row-label intervals. For a row-standard tableau $t$, multiply $x_\eta T_{d(t)}$ successively by these symmetrizers and straighten modulo $I^{\rhd\eta}$. The row calculation is as follows. Once rows before $j$ agree with $t^\eta$, let $\beta_s$ count the labels of $B_j$ in row $s\ge j$; $\sum\beta_s=\eta_j$. Sort these labels in row-reading order to obtain $u$, so $t=uw$ with $w\in S_{B_j}$ and additive length. Therefore multiplication by $x_{B_j}$ first contributes $Q^{\ell(w)}$. The row-parabolic intersection on these labels is $S_{\beta_j}\times\cdots\times S_{\beta_k}$. Expanding its length-additive cosets gives the further factor $[\beta]!_Q$: each common intersection permutation contributes its inversion weight. After removing this intersection, the remaining sum belongs to the two-sided row ideal for the composition $(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{j-1},\eta_j,\eta_j-\beta_j,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$, with zero parts omitted. This is the finite row-double-coset calculation in [F5], using no factorial inversion. If its sorted partition does not lie below $\eta$, its intersection with $I^{\unrhd\eta}$ has only strictly higher shapes and this term vanishes in the cell. Otherwise its prefix inequality at $j+1$ gives $\beta_j\ge\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}$ (the first $j-1$ parts are unchanged, and sorting can only increase the indicated prefix). Straightening retains the now fixed first $j$ canonical rows: maximal prefix counts on those rows cannot be raised further. This proves the same row calculation inductively for every $j$. All coefficients remain in $A$. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. Every such node was addable before the block: adding an $i$-node creates new addable corners only of residues $i+1,i-1$, distinct from $i$ for $e\ge2$. Starting with the empty diagrams, step 1.3 inductively shows its shape dominates $\delta_l$ at every completed block, and hence its final shape dominates $\eta$. No strictly lower shape has the word of $t_\eta$, and no same-shape tableau uniqueness is asserted. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose $P_\xi$ for the word of $t_\eta$. It has nonzero image on $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and zero image on every $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\lhd\eta$, by steps 1.2 and 2.1. Therefore it has zero image on their form quotients. Apply the exact projection to a composition series of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$. Some constituent has nonzero image; by [F1] and [F4] it is a nonzero $D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\unlhd\eta$. The exclusion forces $\rho=\eta$, proving the restricted Murphy quotient nonzero over the original field. This is a joint-word and cellular-support proof, not an import of cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$ for some $j$, every surviving term at that row has $\beta_j\ge e$ by step 1.4 and is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Later multiplication and straightening cannot remove this polynomial factor. Every Gram entry is the coefficient of $x_\eta$ in $x_\eta T_{d(s)}T_{d(t)}^*x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes; first expand its middle factor in the row-module basis and apply the proved row calculation. Thus every entry is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Specializing $Q$ to $q$ makes that factor zero, so the entire Murphy form vanishes and $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)=0$. This concerns a common divisor of entries, not a product-of-hooks formula for a determinant. Combining with step 3.1 proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. [F1, F5, step 1.4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For $e>n$, including infinity, distinct standard tableaux of any shapes have distinct full diagonal words. At their first unequal step the preceding diagram has size $a-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents differ by a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $a\le n$, so their q-integers differ. Induction recovers every next node. Consequently every tableau word of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ occurs in no strictly lower cell. Exact projections as in step 3.1 and diagonal multiplicity one in [F4] show that all $\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ flag factors occur in $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$; thus this quotient has the full cell dimension and its form radical is zero. In particular at $e=\infty$ every partition is restricted and has nonzero quotient. At $n=0$ the unique cell is $F$ with norm one. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Establish the complete semisimplicity clause. Put $f_\eta=\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, with zero for a zero quotient. The Murphy basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient its nondegenerate form and the cell law supply all rank-one operators. Since the cells are right modules, their action gives a surjective algebra map $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}(\eta))^{\mathrm{op}}$, a full matrix algebra after transpose. Its kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals: equality would give the same matrix-algebra simple module, contradicting [F1]. They are pairwise comaximal. Their finite product map is surjective: for each kernel $I_a$ and each other $I_b$ choose $u_{ab}\in I_b$ congruent to one modulo $I_a$, multiply over $b\ne a$, and use these elements to isolate each prescribed matrix component. Its kernel is the radical by the complete simple list and [F6]. Hence $\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2$. Step 4.2 makes this equal to $\dim H$ when $e>n$, giving an isomorphism with a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the one-dimensional Murphy row cell has norm $[n]!_q=0$, since $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient dimension is zero while its cell dimension is one; every other $d_\eta\le f_\eta$. The dimension sum is therefore strictly smaller and $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. This proves both directions of part 3 without any claim that some Specht module must be reducible. [F1, F5, F6, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Apply the same exact involution to every Murphy quotient: $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is nonzero exactly when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero quotients remain pairwise distinct absolutely simple and complete by [F1] and [F2]. This proves parts 1 and 2, and step 5.1 gives part 3. At $q=1$, [F6] gives precisely the ordinary $p$-regular group classification, including characteristic two; no splitting or semisimplicity assumption was made. All selections and polynomial computations were finite, so no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: The type-A Hecke decomposition matrix is dominance unitriangular
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For
$\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$
the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module
$S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]],
[[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$
where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of
$S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates
$\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is
unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the
entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and simple quotients $D^{\mu}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), together with the dominance order on partitions of $n$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ whenever $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$, [F1] and [F4] identify the same ordinary group labels; over a splitting p-modular system this agrees with [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] within that supplier's hypotheses. The present proof establishes the bound over every field. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎
